title: Private lender Merricks traps investor cash for two more years
full_text:
Investors in Regal Partners-backed private lender Merricks Capital will be waiting two more years to get their money back from its flagship fund, after it gated redemptions a year ago.
Merricks has returned just $88m out of $242m investors have been trying to pull out from the $1.1bn Partners Fund since July last year.
At the time, Merricks told investors it was delaying redemptions due to a lack of “unallocated cash” in a major liquidity squeeze for the strategy whose capital was fully deployed.
Instead of handing back their money, Merricks put investors into a run-off class that pays distributions as investors await their payout. Their capital is not used to back new lending.
Investors were told in July 2025 they would be paid out as cash came in, either from new investors or as loans were repaid.
“Those investors get their in-specie share of assets, and they’ll have their cash returned to them over the next 18 to 24 months,” Regal chief executive Brendan O’Connor told The Australian.
Merricks managing director Geoff Davis said investors were getting about 50 per cent of their investment back within 12 months, on average, with the remainder to be staggered over the coming two years.
No money was paid out in the June quarter due to a handful of loan repayments that were delayed, he confirmed.
“There were three loans that represent around 10 per cent of the fund that were forecast to repay. One’s relating to a bank refinance that was delayed, another’s relating to a property settlement that again was delayed with an institutional purchaser,” Mr Davis said.
“The money needs to come back in order for it to be paid out to these investors, and if it doesn’t come back, because delays can happen, then we just have to update investors,” he said.
Merricks is expecting to make a partial payout to investors in the run-off class in the September quarter but, again, that is conditional on loan repayments coming through.
Regal acquired Merricks in June 2024 for $235m as part of a broader M&A spree by the funds manager. The acquisition came right as cracks were starting to appear in the booming private lending sector.
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission has grown increasingly concerned about the local private credit market, estimated at about $188bn, as tighter liquidity, emerging borrower stress and credit deterioration appear.
Beleaguered property developer Bathla Group, which collapsed into administration on Tuesday, is the latest casualty. Merricks is not exposed to the Western Sydney property developer.
Regal’s Mr O’Connor downplayed concerns about a looming crunch in private lending, saying there was still strong demand from foreign investors looking to put their money to work in Australia.
“Private credit is not a dirty word from our perspective. We’re seeing an increased demand for offshore investors seeking the private credit loans that we’re originating in increasing volume. These are institutional investors.
“It’s really in that sort of mass affluent and retail channel that is responding to this mismatch of liquidity expectations. Some people think private credit can be a short-term investment when really part of your return for private credit is taking a degree of illiquidity risk. The big institutional investors understand that and are continuing to demand the credit that we’re originating, but there are some headwinds within the retail segment domestically,” Mr O’Connor said.
